title: 3Sum Closest
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triplet directly versus sorting and two pointers tracking the closest sum.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an array nums and an integer target, find the sum of three integers in nums that is closest to target, and return that sum. Exactly one such closest sum is assumed to exist.

blocks.caption: Sort the array, fix one value, then two pointers track the closest sum seen so far

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Same 3-value structure as 3Sum, but \"closest\" instead of \"exact\"","Reuse 3Sum's sort-plus-two-pointer core, just swap the equality check for a distance comparison"],["No exact match may exist at all","Track the best, smallest-distance, sum seen so far, rather than stopping only at an exact hit"],["An exact match, if found, can never be beaten","Return immediately the moment the sum exactly equals target, a safe early exit"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an array nums and an integer target, find the sum of three integers in nums that is closest to target, and return that sum. Exactly one such closest sum is assumed to exist.

blocks.title: Analogy: Getting as Close as Possible to a Target Weight With Three Items
blocks.text: Like picking exactly three items from a shelf whose combined weight comes as close as possible to a target weight, without necessarily hitting it exactly.

blocks.caption: Find the triplet whose sum is closest to the target, not necessarily equal to it

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [-1, 2, 1, -4], target = 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["-1 plus 2 plus 1 equals 2, which is the closest sum to 1 among all triplets","closer than any other combination","2 is only 1 away from the target, and no other triplet in this array produces a sum with a smaller distance to 1"],["Answer","2","This triplet's sum is the closest achievable value to the target"]]}

blocks.text: Example: nums = [0, 0, 0], target = 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The only possible triplet is 0, 0, 0, summing to 0","the closest (and only) sum available","With exactly 3 elements, there is only one possible triplet to consider at all"],["Answer","0","The single available triplet's sum is trivially the closest, since there is nothing to compare it against"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: nums has exactly 3 elements
With exactly three elements, there is only one possible triplet, so its sum is trivially the closest sum, regardless of the target.
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every triplet, notice this problem is 3Sum wearing a slightly different hat: instead of asking "does a triplet sum to exactly target", it asks "which triplet's sum is nearest to target", a small change in the success condition that leaves the underlying search structure completely unchanged.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: 3Sum's core technique, fix one value, then use two pointers on the sorted remainder to search for the other two, works regardless of whether the goal is an exact match or a closest approximation, since the pointer movement logic only depends on comparing the current sum to the target, not on requiring equality.

Observation 2: The only real change needed is what happens at each comparison: instead of stopping only on an exact match, the algorithm now tracks the best, smallest absolute distance to target, sum seen at any point during the entire scan, updating it whenever a closer one is found.

Observation 3: An exact match, when one happens to exist, is still meaningful: a distance of exactly 0 can never be beaten by any other triplet, so the search can safely return immediately the moment that happens, without waiting to exhaust every remaining fixed value.

Observation 4: Because the two-pointer movement rule is unchanged, the same guarantee 3Sum relies on, that moving the correct pointer never skips over a potentially-better pair, still holds here, just judged by "closer to target" instead of "equal to target".

Whenever a familiar sum-matching problem is relaxed from "exact" to "closest", keep the exact same search structure and pointer logic, and simply replace the success condition with a running best-distance comparison.

This is a clean example of recognizing that a problem's underlying search strategy and its success condition are two separable things: changing one, exact match to closest match, does not require changing the other, sort plus fix-one-value plus two pointers.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every triplet directly, computing its sum and comparing how close it is to the target, keeping track of the closest one found.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every triplet of indices, compute the sum of the three values.
Compare the absolute difference between that sum and target against the best difference found so far.
Keep the sum with the smallest difference.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: best_sum is initialized using the first three actual elements of nums, not an arbitrary sentinel value like 0 or infinity, since it must already be a genuinely achievable triplet sum before any comparison can be trusted.

The distance comparison checks the absolute difference between each sum and the target, not the sums themselves, since "closest" is fundamentally a question about magnitude of difference, not raw value.
Every triplet is checked with no early exit, since without sorting, there is no guarantee about which direction to search, so nothing can be safely skipped.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every triplet is directly checked, so the true closest sum is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), checking every triplet.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: just like 3Sum, sorting the array first and using two pointers for the remaining pair after fixing one value turns the cubic search into a quadratic one.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Checking every triplet blindly wastes the same opportunity 3Sum's brute force wastes: once one value is fixed, finding the best remaining pair is really a sorted two-value search, and a sorted two-value search never needs to try every pair, since comparing the current sum to the target directly tells us which single direction, larger or smaller, could possibly improve things. The only adjustment needed for "closest" instead of "exact" is to keep comparing every candidate sum against the best one seen so far, rather than stopping the search only when equality happens to occur. Since exact equality, a distance of 0, is the best any sum could ever achieve, hitting it is still worth an immediate return, but failing to hit it exactly no longer means the search failed, it simply means the running best-so-far comparison keeps going.

Sort the array, fix one value at a time, and use two pointers on the rest to search for the pair that brings the total sum as close to target as possible, moving the pointer in the direction that reduces the distance to target at each step, and updating the best sum found along the way.
9. Optimized Solution
Sort the array, fix the first value, then two pointers on the remainder, always tracking the closest sum seen.
Dry run for sorted nums = [-4, -1, 1, 2], target = 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Fixed value","Left","Right","Current sum (distance)","Action and why"],"rows":[["-4","-1","2","-3 (distance 4)","Sum too small compared to target 1, move left inward; -3 is far from 1, so best_sum stays at its initial value or updates only slightly"],["-4","1","2","-1 (distance 2)","Sum too small, move left inward; -1 is closer to 1 than -3 was, so best_sum updates to -1"],["-1","1","2","2 (distance 1)","Closest so far, distance 1, sum too large relative to target, move right inward; best_sum updates to 2"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: fix one value, two pointers on the rest, tracking the closest sum found

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the outer loop over fixed values times the two pointer scan for each one.
Space: O(log n) to O(n) depending on the sort.
Why This Works

The two-pointer movement rule, move left up when the sum is too small, move right down when too large, still correctly explores every pair that could possibly be closer to the target than one already checked, since it relies only on the sorted order of the remaining values, never on requiring an exact match. Because every candidate sum, not just an eventual exact match, is compared against the running best, the algorithm is guaranteed to have seen the true closest sum by the time every fixed value has had its own two-pointer scan completed, or to have exited early the moment a perfect, unbeatable match was found.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison result","What happens"],"rows":[["The current sum is strictly closer to target than best_sum","best_sum is updated to the current sum, since a strictly closer sum has just been found"],["The current sum equals target exactly","Return immediately; no other sum could ever be closer than an exact match"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: best_sum is initialized once, before the main loop, using the first three elements of the now-sorted array, guaranteeing it always starts as a real, valid triplet sum.

The distance comparison happens on every single iteration of the two-pointer loop, not just when a pair is first found, since every candidate sum, whether ultimately kept or discarded by the pointer movement, is a genuine data point worth comparing.

The early return on an exact match is placed immediately after the distance comparison, since the best_sum update must happen first even in the exact-match case, before short-circuiting the rest of the search.
The final branch, moving right inward, runs whenever the sum is not less than target, correctly covering the case where it exceeds the target once the exact-match case has already returned.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (check every triplet)","O(n cubed)","O(1)","Every triplet is directly computed and compared, without exploiting sortedness"],["Optimized (sort, fix one value, two pointers)","O(n squared)","O(log n) to O(n) for the sort","One outer loop over fixed values, each paired with a single linear two-pointer scan"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This is a direct variant of the 3Sum pattern, replacing the exact match check with a running "closest so far" comparison, and the early return on an exact match is a small but valid optimization since no sum could ever be closer to the target than an exact match.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to initialize best_sum with a valid real triplet sum before the search begins, instead of an arbitrary placeholder value like 0 or infinity that could incorrectly appear closer than any real achievable sum.
Not returning immediately on an exact match, missing a small but valid early exit opportunity, and doing unnecessary extra work for the remainder of the scan.

Comparing raw sums instead of their absolute distance to target, which would incorrectly treat a sum far below the target as "better" than one slightly above it, when in fact distance, not direction, is what determines closeness.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Point out explicitly that this is 3Sum with the equality check replaced by a distance comparison, since recognizing the shared structure is more valuable than treating this as a brand new problem from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the sum or combination closest to a target, not necessarily exact" points toward reusing the exact-match algorithm's search structure unchanged, just replacing the success condition with a running best-distance comparison, plus an early exit if an exact match happens to occur.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you return the actual triplet, not just its sum? Store the three values, or their indices, alongside best_sum, updating all of them together whenever a strictly closer sum is found.

How would this generalize to 4Sum Closest? Wrap one more "fix a value" loop around this exact same core, exactly as 4Sum wraps an extra loop around 3Sum, keeping the same running best-distance tracking.

What if multiple triplets could tie for the closest distance? The problem as stated assumes a unique closest sum exists; if ties needed to be reported, every sum achieving the current best distance would need to be collected, not just the first one found.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Direct variant of 3Sum, replacing its exact-match success condition with a running closest-distance comparison, while keeping the identical sort-plus-two-pointer search structure.
Same "best-so-far tracking during a two-pointer scan" technique as Container With Most Water, just optimizing for minimum distance to a target instead of maximum area.
Same "an exact or best-possible match justifies an early exit" logic seen in many optimization search problems, where reaching a theoretical best bound ends the search immediately.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n squared) time, O(log n) to O(n) space from sorting.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sort, fix one value, two pointers on the rest, tracking the closest sum seen so far
Core Idea: 3Sum Closest reuses 3Sum's exact search structure, replacing the exact-match success condition with a running smallest-distance-to-target comparison
Time: O(n squared)
Space: O(log n) to O(n), from the sort

Most Important Observation: A search strategy and its success condition are separable; relaxing "exact match" to "closest match" only requires changing what counts as success, not how the search itself proceeds
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Same 3Sum scan, just chase the smallest distance instead of a perfect zero
